title: Deep-ICE: The first globally optimal algorithm for empirical risk minimization of two-layer maxout and ReLU networks
claim: A globally optimal solver finds a decision boundary with fewer misclassifications than the standard gradient-based baseline on identical data.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, left-to-right, 0-1 loss reported in captions
description: Two side-by-side 2-D scatter plots show the same real dataset. Blue crosses mark the positive class, which forms a large cluster in the upper middle and right. Red circles mark the negative class, which sits in the lower left. Each panel shades the plane blue and pink to show the predicted class regions, and a thick black line marks the ReLU decision boundary. In panel (a), labeled Deep-ICE with 0-1 loss 16, the boundary has a kink. It bends around the negative cluster and leaves few red points on the wrong side. In panel (b), labeled gradient descent with 0-1 loss 25, the boundary is a nearly straight diagonal line that cuts through the red points and misclassifies more of them. Both panels share a legend and similar axes. The eye goes first to the black boundary and the pink region, then to the loss numbers in the captions.
caption: The global optimal solution of a rank-2 maxout network with one neuron on a real-world dataset containing $N=704$ data items in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.
abstract: This paper introduces the first globally optimal algorithm for the empirical risk minimization problem of two-layer maxout and ReLU networks, i.e., minimizing the number of misclassifications. The algorithm has a worst-case time complexity of $O\left(N^{DK+1}\right)$, where $K$ denotes the number of hidden neurons and $D$ represents the number of features. It can be can be generalized to accommodate arbitrary computable loss functions without affecting its computational complexity. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithm provides provably exact solutions for small-scale datasets. To handle larger datasets, we introduce a heuristic method that reduces the data size to a manageable scale, making it feasible for our algorithm. This extension enables efficient processing of large-scale datasets and achieves significantly improved performance in both training and prediction, compared to state-of-the-art approaches (neural networks trained using gradient descent and support vector machines), when applied to the same models (two-layer networks with fixed hidden nodes and linear models).
